title: The Three Principles of Redux
description: Learn the three fundamental principles that make Redux predictable and easy to reason about.

data.text: Redux is built on three simple but powerful principles. Understanding them is the key to writing idiomatic Redux code, no matter how complex your application becomes. These principles are not arbitrary rules; they exist to make your app's state predictable, debuggable, and easy to reason about.

data.title: Why Principles Matter
data.text: Every Redux pattern, tool, and best practice is derived from these three principles. If you understand them deeply, the rest of Redux becomes a natural extension of this foundation.

The **state** of your entire application is stored in a single object tree within a single **store**. This makes it easy to inspect, persist, and serialize the state. It also means you have one place to look when debugging.

data.title: Single Store
data.content: All state lives in one store object

data.text: The only way to change the state is to **dispatch an action**, which is a plain object describing what happened. This prevents direct state mutation from anywhere in the app and ensures that every change has a traceable record.

data.title: Dispatching Actions
data.content: Never mutate state directly; always dispatch an action

data.text: Principle 3: Changes are Made by Pure Functions

To specify how the state tree is transformed by actions, you write pure **reducers**. A reducer takes the previous state and an action, and returns the next state. Because reducers are pure, they are predictable and easy to test.

terms.definition: A plain JavaScript object that holds all the data for your application at a given point in time.
The single object that holds the application's state and provides methods to read, dispatch, and subscribe.
A plain object with a `type` field that describes what happened in the application.
A pure function that takes the current state and an action, and returns the next state.

cards.title: Multiple stores (Bad)
cards.description: Splitting state across multiple stores makes synchronizing data hard and breaks the single source of truth.

cards.title: Direct mutation (Bad)
cards.description: Modifying state outside a reducer bypasses the action log and breaks time-travel debugging.

cards.title: Pure reducers (Good)
cards.description: Reducers that only return new state without side effects keep the data flow predictable and testable.

cards.title: Action-driven updates (Good)
cards.description: All state changes flow through dispatched actions, creating a clear audit trail of every update.

data.title: Spot the Violation
data.description: Given a small code snippet, identify which of the three principles is being violated and explain how to fix it.
steps: Identify which principle is broken (single source of truth, read-only state, or pure reducer)
Rewrite the snippet so it follows all three principles
Verify your fix would work with Redux DevTools time-travel
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to name the violated principle, explain why it is a problem, and provide a corrected version that uses a single store, dispatched actions, and a pure reducer.

data.content: Identify the principle that this code violates

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Single source of truth: one store for the whole app
State is read-only: only actions change state
Changes are made by pure reducer functions
Following these principles makes your app predictable and testable
data.takeaway: The three principles are the foundation that makes Redux predictable, debuggable, and easy to test.
